name: Papaya leaf extract (Carica papaya)
short: Animal data raise liver and reproductive toxicity concerns with long-term use; a review cautions in pregnancy and liver impairment and lists drug interactions. Short trials: mostly mild stomach upset.
text: A 2021 systematic scoping review of 41 articles (23 clinical studies, 5 ongoing trials and 13 preclinical studies) found papaya leaf, as juice or a standardised aqueous extract, well tolerated by adults for short durations (under five days), with minor gastrointestinal side effects most commonly reported; it noted concerns about liver toxicity and reproductive toxicity with long-term use, supported by animal studies, cautioned use in pregnancy and in people with liver impairment, and listed unfavourable herb-drug interactions with metformin, glimepiride, digoxin, ciprofloxacin and artemisinin (the abstract does not say whether these come from human or laboratory studies). In a 300-patient double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in dengue fever, a few gastrointestinal adverse events such as nausea and vomiting occurred at similar rates in both groups, and a meta-analysis of nine controlled dengue studies of Carica papaya extract (the abstract does not name the plant part) found that serious adverse events were not reported. In a phase III placebo-controlled trial in 198 analysed patients with low platelets caused by cancer chemotherapy, there were no grade 3 or grade 4 treatment-related adverse events with papaya leaf extract. The dengue trial gave the extract for five days and the chemotherapy trial for up to 10 days.
